item.title: IDEA: You’ve Heard “Be Bold, Start Cold.” But How Cold is Too Cold?
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine
Hike long enough and you’ll inevitably hear the phrase, “Be Bold, Start Cold.” It’s catchy, easy to remember and generally good advice for anyone starting out early in the morning. On its surface, it’s simple: Don’t bother wearing a ton of layers you’ll take off the first fifteen minutes into your walk. Starting a little colder means skipping the first half mile shed and letting your body naturally warm up to its resting active temperature. But how cold is too cold? How do you tell the difference between a chill that’ll wear off by the first switchback and a sign you should’ve kept your jacket on? Does the first fifteen minutes warming up do more harm than good? When I asked Mike Tipton, a professor of human and applied physiology at the University of Portsmouth, about the old mountaineering phrase, he generally agreed with the principal but thought it needed a bit more nuance. Tipton has spent four decades studying how the body regulates its temperature, and part of his research looks at what happens to hands and feet during prolonged exposure to cold. His studies have informed the British Royal Navy’s approach to cooling overheated officers, and he’s worked with the U.S. Coast Guard to develop a model that estimates how long someone lost at sea might survive in cold water. His advice for hikers was simple: have a smart layering strategy. He didn’t take issue with “Be Bold,” but thought hikers should take more care when it comes to starting cold. So how do you tell whether you’re underdressed or overprepared? We talked to Tipton, Appalachian Mountain Club guide Marielle Fibish, and western North Carolina search and rescue team member Nancy East about what to wear for the first mile of a winter hike, how to tell when it’s time to add or shed a layer, and when you’re better off starting warm. For East, a good starting point is how you feel while you’re waiting for a hiking partner to lace up their boots. Can you stand around comfortably for a few minutes? “It’s the type of chill that fresh clothes from the dryer would immediately quell,” she says. Tipton suggests paying attention to your hands. As your body cools, blood flow to your fingers decreases, which can make something as simple as working a zipper harder. In his view, “the ideal place to be is where your extremities feel warm, but you’re not producing vast amounts of sweat.” Once you’re walking, pay attention to which way things are headed. Is that slight chill wearing off, or are your fingers getting colder with every switchback? “If my hands are getting cold, I’m shivering, or I’m not generating enough body heat to feel comfortable after several minutes of hiking, I’ll add a layer,” East says. When Fibish gets dressed for a winter hike in the White Mountains, she checks the forecast, then dresses as though it’s about 10°F warmer. Say it’s 20°F at the trailhead. Fibish dresses the way she would for a walk in 30°F weather. The puffy, shell, and extra mittens are all coming with her. They just get to ride in her bag for the first mile. One mistake Fibish sees is hikers reaching for the same outfit they’d wear to the ski hill. “Insulated snow pants and jackets are great for downhill skiing and making snowmen, but they can be too warm for other outdoor winter activities like hiking or Nordic skiing,” she says. For hiking, she builds her outfit around a close-fitting wool top and bottoms, with hiking or soft-shell pants over the base layer. A separate fleece gives her some warmth she can shed on the first climb without losing her protection from the wind. Fibish also thinks about who’s coming along. If you’re breaking trail for the group, you might be glad you left your fleece in your pack. If you tend to run cold and expect to spend some of that first mile waiting for friends, you might want to keep it on. Give yourself five or ten minutes of walking, Fibish says, and you’ll have a better sense of how well you guessed. For Fibish, the first cue to lose a layer is a little tingle of warmth building under her clothes. Sometimes slipping off her hat or hiking in glove liners is enough. On a sustained climb, she might stop to take off her fleece. As Tipton explains, your working muscles produce heat. Taking off a layer lets more of that heat escape into the air, so your body can regulate its core temperature with less sweating. Your hands can tell you when it’s time to add a layer, too. As your body cools, Tipton explains, blood vessels near the skin narrow to conserve heat in your core. That leaves less warm blood flowing to your fingers. East pays attention when her hands start getting colder, even if she’s still walking. She’ll also pull on a layer if she starts to shiver or if several minutes of hiking haven’t warmed her up. “I don’t wait until I’m genuinely cold to do something about it,” she says. A snack break is one layer change you can see coming. Once you stop climbing, your muscles produce less heat, but sweat evaporating from your damp shirt keeps cooling you. If the wind picks up at the top, East pulls on a fleece or puffy, followed by a windproof layer, before she settles in to eat. Jacket first, sandwich second. East likes to know what those first ten minutes of walking are going to look like. If it’s especially cold, wet, or windy, she’ll start a little warmer. Same goes for an exposed stretch of trail: If the climb starts somewhere on the other side of a windy meadow, you’ve still got the meadow to cross. You can take your jacket off when you get into an area with more coverage. So is “be bold, start cold” good advice? If you’re about to head uphill and you know you’ll be peeling off your fleece by the first switchback, sure. If you’re already cold standing there, you can keep it on and plan to stop a few minutes up the trail. On early starts in the Himalayas, Tipton’s group would stop five minutes up the trail so everyone could adjust their layers. It’s advice worth taking. Pick a spot a few minutes up the trail while everyone’s still gearing up. That way, nobody has to be the first to ask, “Mind if I stop and take this thing off?” East has her own version of the phrase: “Start cool, but don’t stay cold.”

item.title: REVIEW: Norwegian Luna cruise ship review: What to expect on board
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Is Norwegian Luna the best big new ship sailing out of Miami? For someone looking for a vessel that feels more refined and upscale than what is typical among big Miami-based ships, it just might be. (Its sister ship, Norwegian Aqua, also sails from Miami.) As I saw during a week on board in October, Norwegian Luna has an elevated design compared to many of the big new ships sailing out of Miami, giving it an elegance that stands out among the competition. That said, for someone who just wants the widest array of onboard amusements, entertainment and nightlife that they can find on a cruise ship, the choice gets harder. Although its large, the eight-month-old Norwegian Luna — the latest in Norwegian Cruise Line's Prima Plus class — is notably smaller than the other big new ships that it is up against in Miami. That means there's less room for the wide range of attractions you'll find on those vessels. Unlike two of its biggest rivals in the market, Royal Caribbean's Icon of the Seas and MSC Cruises' MSC World America, for instance, it lacks a water park area with multiple waterslides on its top deck (though it does have one large water attraction, the Aqua Slidecoaster). It also has fewer and smaller main pool areas. That's a real strike against it for families with kids, in particular. As someone who generally prefers more intimate and elegant ships, I know which side of the trade-off I'm on. If it were my money, I'd lean toward Norwegian Luna. It's the perfect big ship for me. But read on to see if it's right for you. Unveiled in March, Norwegian Luna is the second ship in Norwegian's new Prima Plus Class of vessels, following the year-old Norwegian Aqua. These two ships, along with two similar but slightly smaller Prima Class vessels that debuted in 2022 and 2023, are smaller than the ships that Norwegian launched just before them, which is a bit unusual. Most of Norwegian's competitors, such as Royal Caribbean and MSC Cruises, have been rolling out ever bigger ships, loaded with ever more onboard attractions and venues. Norwegian Luna by the numbers: For now, Norwegian Luna mostly operates seven-night voyages to the Caribbean out of Miami on Saturdays, competing head-to-head with new ships from Royal Caribbean and MSC Cruises (Icon of the Seas and MSC World America) that are much bigger. Those two ships, notably, are 59% and 38% bigger than Luna, respectively, allowing for a lot more onboard venues of all kinds, from decktop attractions to showrooms, restaurants and bars. On the flip side, Norwegian Luna's smaller size, coupled with its elevated design, generally contributes to a more intimate and elegant feel — a significant differentiator. I say "generally," as Norwegian Luna's more elegant feel is sometimes punctured by aggressive upselling and extra charges that are incongruous with the ship's overall vibe. It's not a dealbreaker, but it's off-putting at times and something you need to be prepared for going into a sailing. Cabins are a strong point on Norwegian Luna. The majority of balcony cabins (the biggest category of cabins on the ship) are surprisingly spacious at 358 square feet, with a clean-lined, modern design and solid storage. I particularly love the bathrooms, which offer larger showers than you sometimes get on mass-market ships as well as a clever pivot door that makes them easy to enter. Balcony cabins account for about 57% of Norwegian Luna's 1,813 cabins. But there are also 140 oceanview cabins without balconies of various sizes and 424 windowless "inside" cabins that offer a modern design with solid storage. The latter category includes 73 very small but perfect-for-one solo cabins, known as Studios, in a keycard-access-only solo area with its own lounge — a Norwegian signature. Norwegian has leaned into the solo cruise market in recent years with these exclusive solo areas, and the cabins are in high demand. Book one early if you want one. Norwegian Luna is also home to one of the line's signature The Haven suite complexes. These are separate, keycard-access-only enclaves found on many Norwegian ships that not only have a wide range of lovely suites but also their own private restaurants, lounges and bars, and outdoor sun and pool decks. On Norwegian Luna, this complex (tied with the one on Norwegian Aqua as the biggest in the fleet) fills the top four decks of the back of the ship, accessible via its own private elevator. It's truly wonderful. Staying in one of its suites — there are 123, including 25 Owner's Suites that measure up to an astounding 2,100 square feet — feels like staying in a completely different, far more upscale vessel. Among my favorite features of Norwegian Luna's Haven area is its cozy bar, which offers a much-upgraded bar experience to what you'll find anywhere else on the ship. There are higher-end spirits and creative craft cocktails made by some of the best bartenders at sea. In addition to the suites in The Haven, you'll find additional suites and penthouses outside the area that also come with extra privileges but not all the perks that Haven guests receive. Pro tip: If you are sensitive to noise, steer clear of cabins with connecting doors to adjacent cabins (you'll find them noted on Norwegian Luna's deck plans). Even when closed, their imperfect seals will cause you to hear noise from the cabin next door. Norwegian ships have always been known for a wide range of restaurant choices, and Norwegian Luna is no exception. It has more than a dozen sit-down eateries, ranging from a super-casual food hall to a high-end steakhouse — some quite good for a big, mass-market ship. Just be warned that the restaurant scene on Norwegian Luna is one of the areas where you'll encounter a lot of upcharges, with both high cover charges for some restaurants and additional charges for individual menu items that can really push up the bill. Among the priciest eateries on board are Norwegian's two signature restaurants, Cagney's Steakhouse (found on every Norwegian ship) and the French-focused Le Bistro (found on nearly every Norwegian ship). Both have cover charges of $60 per person that rise to $72 per person with a mandatory 20% gratuity; that price can climb even higher if you order an item with an upcharge. Both are elegant and upscale, and serve quality dishes, as does Palomar, which serves seafood-focused Mediterranean cuisine for the same $60 cover charge. I highly recommend Palomar's whole fish-for-two baked in salt, which is well worth its additional $25 charge ($30 with the mandatory gratuity) — not just because it's a showy dish that tastes as good as it looks, but because it's deboned tableside, adding some tableside theatrics to the evening. Other extra-charge eateries include Los Lobos ($40 per person), which dishes out Mexican cuisine; Nama Sushi & Sashimi ($50 per person), for its namesake Japanese cuisine; Japanese hibachi restaurant Hasuki ($60 per person); and Thai-centered Sukothai ($50 per person). All of these have mandatory 20% gratuity charges on top of their cover charges, as does Onda by Scarpetta, which is an Italian eatery ($40 per person) with ties to New York City's high-end Scarpetta restaurant. The latter is one eatery I'd skip, as the cuisine is spotty and the service more rushed than relaxing. (Despite ordering four courses, we were barely there an hour as the dishes were raced out to us one on top of the other.) For those keeping to a tight budget, there are fortunately plenty of solid included-in-the-fare options on Norwegian Luna, too. The real standout here is Indulge Food Hall, a casual, multi-outlet venue with separate stands and counters serving tapas, Indian dishes, noodles, vegetarian bowls, barbecue, Latin and Mexican food, and rotisserie items. Some of these items, particularly the Indian dishes (which include chicken tikka made in an actual tandoor oven), are quite good for a free-on-a-ship casual eatery. Pro tip: If you're sitting at one of the many tables scattered around Indulge Food Hall, you can order from any of the stands and counters via a tabletop tablet. But if you sit at the counter for any particular food outlet, you can only order from that outlet's menu. Pick your seats with that in mind. A sleeper hit with no extra charge is The Local Bar and Grill, which has both indoor and outdoor seating with a casual diner vibe. It's open around the clock for table-served American comfort food (think: burgers, chicken wings and nachos). But most importantly, for me, it's a calmer and less crowded place for breakfast than the seemingly always-jammed buffet at the top of the ship (more on that in a moment). I loved sitting in its outdoor area on sea days, overlooking the water, for a leisurely eggs-bacon-and-toast breakfast served by a friendly waiter — a much more civilized experience than the buffet. By contrast, the shiptop buffet called Surfside is an included-in-the-fare outlet to avoid. While a convenient quick-bite option for passengers lounging at the pool (it's right next door), it's too small for a ship the size of Norwegian Luna. It has too few tables, too few food stations and too narrow a walkway along the food stations to be a pleasant experience much of the time it's open. Rounding out the included-in-the-fare options are two larger complimentary sit-down restaurants, The Commodore Room and Hudson's. Both offer the same dinner menu, with decent, if not always consistent, offerings and pleasant service. Hudson's is also open for breakfast and lunch. Among the upcharges at both eateries are $20-$30 fees for signature dishes from the ship's Cagney's Steakhouse, such as its ribeye steak ($25). While I'm generally not a fan of the trend toward more upcharges at supposedly included-in-the-fare cruise ship eateries, this does allow for what is one of my favorite dining hacks when sailing on a Norwegian ship: creating an almost-as-good-as-the-real-thing Cagney's steakhouse experience at less than half the price. I order that ribeye and the always-available Caesar salad (nearly identical to the one at Cagney's except you don't get anchovies on top) and a couple of glasses of the included-in-Free-at-Sea-packages Malbec, which is the very same Malbec offered at Cagney's, and pretend I'm at the latter eatery. The total cost, including the mandatory gratuity, is $30 versus $72 per person at Cagney's. No matter where you are on Norwegian Luna, you are never far from a bar. There are more than a dozen of them in the interior parts of the ship alone, plus more on the outside decks. Among the liveliest (and my personal favorite) is the Metropolitan Bar, which stands out for its "zero waste" cocktails featuring such ingredients as syrup made from discarded banana peels. It's bustling every night with live music that ranges from Latin beats to classic '80s rock. The Belvedere Bar at the top level of the atrium is also hopping with live music nightly, as is the Penrose Bar two decks below. (Musicians play at the base of the atrium not far from it.) All three of these bars line high-traffic areas and can get busy. For something more tucked away, quieter and usually less crowded, the side-by-side Whiskey Bar and Swirl Wine Bar offer intimate spaces dedicated strictly to their respective namesake pours. There's also the bar at The Local Bar & Grill mentioned in the restaurant section above, which serves as the casual go-to spot to catch a game over bar bites. Beyond these, you'll find multiple bars servicing the pool and activity areas at the top of the ship as well as every interior entertainment venue, including the main theater and comedy club. Up at the very front of the ship, the Observation Lounge pairs a full bar with sweeping daytime ocean views. What you won't find on Norwegian Luna, unlike on some competitor ships sailing from Miami, is a true craft cocktail venue. The Metropolitan Bar comes the closest with its "zero waste" cocktails. But even here, most drinks are quick-made affairs lacking the house-made ingredients, specialty clear ice and precision construction that has become commonplace at craft bars on land. The Whiskey Bar also has craft elements, including a wide range of whiskeys and knowledgeable bartenders mixing old fashioneds, Boulevardiers and other whiskey drinks with precision. But the venue falls down on things like proper ice for drinks. (They oddly have just 20 large cubes available each night, which disappear fast, resulting in most cocktails coming out with the same small ice cubes found at the basic bars on the pool deck.) For coffee drinkers, a full-size Starbucks in the atrium rounds out the beverage options. Norwegian is no longer the leader in big ship entertainment, following cutbacks over the past three years. All the big-name Broadway shows, from "Jersey Boys" to "Kinky Boots," are gone. But it still offers solid entertainment in its main theaters, including the one on Norwegian Luna. The big crowdpleaser on Norwegian Luna is "Elton: A Celebration of Elton John," a flashy tribute show that strings together John's biggest hits with visual pizzazz that includes elaborate costumes and choreography, special effects and archival footage projected on a back screen. If you're an Elton John fan like me, you'll love it. The other big show in the Luna Theater, "HIKO: Innovation Meets Wonder," is a moody, sci-fi-themed mashup of custom-scored music, dance, showy costumes, 3D projections, lasers and acrobatics (think high-flying trampoline acts and aerial silk routines). It starts out slow but picks up toward the end. There's also a rocking Eagles tribute show in the main theater with a full band, which is another crowd-pleaser. There are also more tribute shows focused on Billy Joel and Fleetwood Mac (the former in the smaller Syd Norman Pour House; the latter at the main theater). And yes, you'll see a theme among the performers Norwegian has chosen for these tribute shows. These are all musical groups that are popular with Baby Boomers and Generation Xers who grew up with them, but have also had a resurgence among younger generations — perfect for Norwegian's wide demographic. One other notable entertainment option is LunaTique Pop Circus, a bawdy, adults-only, cabaret-style nightlife experience set to pop music, with plenty of audience participation. (If the idea of being pulled up on stage terrifies you, don't sit in the front rows.) It's the only show on Norwegian Luna with an extra charge ($45 per person, including four drinks that get served to everyone as part of the show). LunaTique Pop Circus takes place in Improv at Sea, an intimate comedy club that also is the place for stand-up comedy on most nights. While not quite as elaborate as the entertainment on the larger Royal Caribbean and MSC Cruises ships that sail out of Miami on weekends, the above shows have been earning high marks from cruisers since Norwegian Luna debuted and are among the most popular activities on the ship. Just be warned that, because of that popularity, it can sometimes be hard to get a seat for these shows, which is a common complaint among passengers. With just 752 seats, the Luna Theater is small for a ship the size of Norwegian Luna and fills up long before showtime. Ditto for the smaller Syd Norman's Pour House and Improv at Sea venues, which each can hold just 100 or so people. If you want a seat for any of the shows, particularly a good seat near the front, head to the venue at least 45 minutes in advance. Norwegian Luna pool decks and activities Norwegian Luna has a lot to offer on its top decks, particularly in the "family fun" department. The standout attraction is its giant Aqua Slidecoaster water ride. It uses the same magnetic accelerator system found in modern roller coasters to blast you skyward in a raft that then takes you winding back down a meandering waterslide course. It's both tons of fun and completely free. You'll find several more fun family attractions tucked under and around the Aqua Slidecoaster, including a 12-hole, high-tech minigolf course where each stroke of your ball is electronically tracked and you get bonus points for hitting certain targets. It comes with a per-person charge of $5 but is well worth it. Also in this area is The Stadium (free outdoor games including table tennis, bean bag toss and foosball) and the Bull's Eye Bar, which features tech-enhanced darts games. You'll also find the entrance to The Drop, a terrifying-looking dry slide that spirals 10 decks down the side of the ship. It was a hard pass for me, but try it if you're daring. Rounding out this area are a pickleball court and Glow Court — a high-tech sports court with an LED wall that lets you play challenging ball-throwing games (just be careful not to hit your partner with a ball, as I did; you might find yourself in the doghouse). While great fun, these attractions eat up a lot of real estate on the top decks, leaving less room for pool areas. The ship's main pool area, just in front of the Aqua Slidecoaster, feels small for a ship the size of Norwegian Luna (and, indeed, was uncomfortably jammed on sea days during my sailing). One deck up from the pool is the often-crowded Kids' Aqua Park, where little ones can enjoy water sprayers and mini waterslides. The solution to escape the crowds (if you're kid-free, at least) is to spend $289 per person for a weekly pass to the adults-only Vibe Beach Club — a separate, keycard-access-only deck-top lounge area that is roughly the same size as the main pool area but limited to just 166 passengers. It is blissfully uncrowded and quiet compared to the main pool area and has its own bar and hot tubs facing the sea. Pro tip: Splurge for one of the 12 private cabanas at the Vibe Beach Club, which cost a seemingly high $619 per week but come with access for two people, so they're really only about $310 per person. That's just $21 more per person than buying two Vibe passes, and it's a much nicer experience. Alternatively, you can book a cabin in The Haven, which, as noted above, also has its own decktop lounge area (at the back of the ship) with its own pool and bar. Between these two areas (Vibe and The Haven), Norwegian Luna notably has a lot more of its decktop real estate devoted to exclusive upcharge areas than other big ships sailing from Miami. What this effectively means is that the ship offers a bifurcated decktop experience. If you pay up, you will experience something more relaxing and exclusive than you will find on many other big ships. If you don't, the top deck experience might feel less appealing. That said, if you're willing to head down nine decks, you'll find additional outdoor lounge space with lounge chairs and small plunge pools along an outdoor promenade that wraps around the sides of the ships. With a cool South Beach vibe that includes plush circular seats for two surrounded by wading pools, it's an innovative additional outdoor area that is often less crowded than the top-deck pool area. For indoor fun, the family-focused Luna Game Zone near the Observation Lounge offers an array of video, virtual reality and other games (some for free and some for a fee). Plus, for adults, there's a sizable casino with VIP and smoking rooms, as well as slots and table games. Norwegian Luna also has a massive, multilevel spa (the Mandara Spa) with one of the loveliest and most relaxing thermal suites at sea. Accessible for an extra charge, it has a stunning, two-deck-high room with water therapy pools; a separate area that is home to all sorts of therapeutic rooms including Finnish, charcoal and clay saunas, a steam room and a salt room; and a separate, blissfully relaxing room full of heated loungers overlooking the sea. Just be warned that access to the thermal suite costs a sky-high $630 per person for the week (though discounts are sometimes available onboard at the start of the cruise). The spa area is also where you'll find the ship's fitness room, which is free to use and offers plenty of cardio equipment and free weights, but lacks a full range of weight machines. The ship's entertainment staff also programs all sorts of daily activities throughout the ship, including trivia games, karaoke, art and dance classes, and family events. Through at least April 2028, Norwegian Luna will mostly sail seven-night cruises from Miami to the Caribbean, with departures on Saturdays. The exception is during the summer of 2027, when it will reposition to New York for four-, five- and seven-night cruises to Bermuda. When sailing from Miami, the ship operates both Eastern and Western Caribbean itineraries. Eastern Caribbean itineraries typically include stops at Puerto Plata, Dominican Republic; St. Thomas, U.S. Virgin Islands; Tortola, British Virgin Islands; and Great Stirrup Cay, Norwegian's private island in the Bahamas. Western Caribbean itineraries typically bring calls in Roatan, Honduras; Harvest Caye, Belize; and Costa Maya and Cozumel, Mexico. Fares for seven-night Caribbean sailings start at $549 per person, based on double occupancy. Fares for seven-night Bermuda sailings start at $1,229 per person, based on double occupancy. Such pricing is for inside cabins on the most offseason dates. You'll pay more for oceanview and balcony cabins and suites, as well as for sailings on more in-demand weeks. Norwegian Luna is a big new ship that feels more refined and upscale than many of the other big new ships sailing out of Miami. That's in part because of its more elegant design and its (relatively) smaller size. The downside of that smaller size is that the ship doesn't have quite as many onboard attractions — like decktop features, showrooms, restaurants and bars — as some of its competitors. item.title: Yet another giant new cruise ship takes to the sea
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
The cruise world welcomed another giant on Wednesday as MSC Cruises took delivery of one of its largest ships ever, the 216,638-ton MSC World Asia. Built at the massive Chantiers de l'Atlantique shipyard in Saint-Nazaire, France, the 20-deck-high, Asia-themed vessel is the third in the line's new World Class series of ships — by far the biggest ships that MSC Cruises has ever built. Perhaps more notably, it is the tenth largest cruise ship ever built by any line, smaller only than Royal Caribbean's three Icon Class ships and six Oasis Class ships. "Our ambition is simple: To give every guest the best holiday ever," MSC Group executive chairman Pierfrancesco Vago said Wednesday during a dockside ceremony at the Chantiers de l'Atlantique shipyard to mark the vessel's official handover to MSC Cruises. MSC Group is the parent company of MSC Cruises and sister brand Explora Journeys, a luxury line. "We invested in rethinking spaces, developing new concepts and reshaping the experience," Vago added during remarks from a stage set up just in front of the MSC World Asia's bow. Vago noted that 60% of the spaces on MSC World Asia are either new or significantly redesigned as compared to the two World Class ships already sailing, MSC World Europa and MSC World America. Like those two vessels, MSC World Asia has nearly 2,600 rooms and is capable of holding a whopping 6,758 passengers with every berth filled — more than almost any other passenger vessel afloat. It also has similarly massive dimensions with a length of 1,093 feet — the equivalent of nearly four football fields stacked end-to-end — and a width of 154 feet. But many of its interior and exterior venues, including a sprawling decktop water park with multiple waterslides and a record-setting dry slide that drops 11 decks, are different from what you'll find on the earlier World Class ships in ways big and small. Among the most significant changes is the addition of new dining and food concepts, including MSC Cruises' first pan-Asian restaurant and a Venchi chocolate and gelato venue. Like the earlier World Class vessels, the ship also offers a sushi bar, teppanyaki restaurant, American-style steakhouse and a branch of the Italian chain Eataly (currently found only on MSC World America), among 20 dining options in all. In addition to the water park and dry slide, MSC World Asia's top decks offer multiple pool areas; a suspended-over-the-ocean swing ride called The Cliffhangar; and a ropes course. Notable interior features include a three-deck-high dining and entertainment zone called the World Galleria, which is covered by one of the largest LED-lit ceilings at sea. An outdoor extension of this area, called the World Promenade, features more dining and entertainment, plus a new suspended, illuminated Dragon sculpture — part of the ship's Asia theming. The arrival of MSC World Asia marks the latest milestone in MSC Cruises' rapid expansion. With the addition of MSC World Asia, the brand now operates 24 ships, up from just 13 vessels as recently as 2017. It has nine more on order. The ships on the way include five more World Class vessels scheduled for delivery by 2031. Also coming is a new class of four somewhat smaller, 180,000-ton vessels that will be known as the Frontier Class. Wednesday's delivery ceremony included a ceremonial lowering of the Chantiers de l'Atlantique and French flags in front of attendees and the raising of the MSC Cruises flag as well as the flag of Malta, where the vessel is registered. MSC Group chief financial officer Alexa Aponte Vago, who is married to MSC Group executive chairman Pierfrancesco Vago, served as the traditional "godmother" for the event, which included the smashing of a bottle of Champagne against the ship's hull. Joining her husband on stage, Alexa Aponte Vago cut a ceremonial blue ribbon to release the bottle of Champagne against the side of the vessel right on the letter C in its name. While it included a bottle smash, Wednesday's event was not the vessel's official naming. That will take place Saturday in Le Havre, France, at a much larger event. MSC World Asia will then head to the Mediterranean, where it will begin its first cruises with paying passengers on Dec. 4 with a voyage out of Barcelona. The ship initially will operate seven-night Mediterranean voyages that include stops in France, Italy, Malta and Spain. In November 2027, it will reposition to the Southern Caribbean for seven- to 14-night sailings. The itineraries will include stops in Saint Lucia, Grenada, St. Maarten, Antigua and Barbuda, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Dominica, and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines. Founded in 1861, the Chantiers d'Atlantique shipyard in St. Nazaire is one of the world's most famous shipyards, known for building many of the world's largest cruise ships as well as naval vessels and wind-powered commercial ships. Notable vessels built at the shipyard include the SS Normandie, SS France, Cunard's Queen Mary 2 and several of Royal Caribbean's Oasis Class ships. The shipyard has built 20 vessels for MSC Cruises over the past 25 years. It is located at the mouth of the Loire River on the West coast of France. Planning a cruise? Start with these stories:

item.title: REVIEW: This inexpensive Katie Loxton luggage set nails the chocolate brown travel trend – I put it through its paces in NYC
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
Chocolate brown remains the shade du jour – and if you want to work the trend into your airport wardrobe without spending four figures on designer trunks, this little duo by Katie Loxton will certainly do nicely. This inexpensive British brand is best known for its eminently giftable monogrammable handbags and accessories and, recently, it’s been expanding its travel collection too. Now, just in time for Christmas – and with a tidy 25 per cent discount on these items for Black Friday – you can buy its sweet little faux leather Oxford Cabin Suitcase and Milan Handwoven Cabin Bag together as a gift set for your favourite traveller. The set comprises a smooth-grain cabin suitcase, finished with a combination lock and luggage tag, with a textured woven weekender bag in the same rich hue. There is complimentary monogramming available on both pieces and, with a very pleasing price-point of £209.98 for the pair, it’s a purse-friendly way to feel a little more glam on a weekend hop. It looks sweet as can be, but does its real-world performance hold up on a proper long-haul trip? Ahead of a five-night trip to New York City, I put its capacity, manoeuvrability and durability to the test across two transatlantic flights, hectic JFK transfers and a stay at The Lowell on the Upper East Side. Here’s how it held up under pressure. Pros: - The rich chocolate finish is very striking - The Milan bag’s trolley sleeve slide over the suitcase handle - Generous combined cabin capacity comfortably covered me for a five-day city break Cons: - Vegan PU leather requires more care around scuffs than polycarbonate or aluminium - The case wasn’t especially stable when the cabin bag was full and balanced on top and was prone to toppling over The set’s biggest draw. The dark vegan leather looks chic in person, serviceably adding a little polish without a luxury price tag. Does it look like real leather? No. It’s clearly not a Louis Vuitton case but, for the price, it looks decent. I saw several people on the Underground eyeing it up as I returned home, and the monogramming looks really lovely in shiny gold thread. Given the price-point, I was wondering how it would fare being hoisted into overhead lockers, tackling the subway and being loaded into a yellow cab, but after two seven-hour flights and several Manhattan taxi boots, both pieces arrived at my hotel looking good-as-new. The only quibble was a little scuffing on the handles, but that is only noticeable under scrutiny, and not really an issue for me. I’ve never had that problem with a more expensive case but, for a budget option, I was happy with how the Katie Loxton piece held up. Bear in mind that the brand advises avoiding heavy water exposure, so it’s worth keeping an umbrella handy if you’re caught in a sudden downpour. It’s good news if you like a trunk-style case, as the Oxford suitcase has one roomy, well-proportioned 40L compartment with straps to keep folded knitwear and tailoring pinned down, plus a lid with a zipped mesh pocket and two pouches for smaller bits and chargers. I was doubtful that it would do me for a five-day wintery trip in NYC, I confess – and to get everything in, it did take some strategic packing. I squeezed a pair of heels and all my clothes in the carry-on case (impressively, given it didn’t look like it was going to happen at first) and popped my packing cube with my makeup and wash bag, plus my in-flight essentials, in the personal item. I would not, in an ideal world, keep a packing cube of toiletries in a separate case, but I was impressed at the overall capacity the duo afforded me. Given I was taking a longer break, where I would usually bring a check-in suitcase, this was impressive. For a weekend away, this duo would sort you comfortably without having to keep your toiletries separately. Even on my longer getaway, I still had a little breathing room for a couple of buys from Madison Avenue. The underseat bag is equally thoughtful. It measures 25 x 40 x 19cm, so it’s compact enough to slide neatly under the seat in front on most airlines – I had no problem on British Airways – with ample room for passports, headphones and a paperback, plus a spare jumper to keep me warm on a red-eye. It has fold-down side clips designed to help it meet stricter under-seat dimensions, which is handy for short-haul European hops, though clipping them down will trim the bag’s volume, so bear that in mind if you like to stuff your personal item to the max. There’s also a removable strap for wearing it crossbody. It did tip over on a couple of occasions, so I would recommend this case for weekends where you’re hopping from plane to cab with minimal fanfare. I had no bother when using the case solo, but it was less stable when the weekender was stacked on top. It made navigating the subway a little tricky but, again, I concede that I had squeezed it right to its limits – when I took out the pesky packing cube with my toiletries in, the duo felt a lot more stable. Still, the 360-degree spinner wheels glided smoothly across polished hotel marble and the airport, with only a minor grumble on a few cracked pavements. The retractable handle locks into place well, and the bag on top stayed in place securely thanks to the pass-through band – even when I was running for a subway train, which really hasn’t always been the case with more expensive bags I’ve used, so this earned points with me. Katie Loxton’s The Jetsetter Gift Set is a stylish luggage duo at a punchy price tag for something that looks this sweet. It looks at home in a smart hotel lobby, packs a surprising amount in, and makes you feel put together while you’re at it. If you’re a heavy packer you might have to hang onto it to avoid it from taking a tumble, but for shorter hops and city staycations, this is a lovely option. Chocolate not your thing? There are several colours to choose from, and you can also buy the Oxford Cabin Suitcase and Milan Cabin Bag separately to mix and match across shades. We especially like the rich cherry version.
